title: Mahalia Jackson
hookLine: the queen of gospel, who sang at the great civil rights march in the capital

lines: A CROWD DOWN THE NATIONAL MALL.
cards: A crowd stretches down the National Mall, all the way along the reflecting pool. It's hot. Then a woman steps up to the microphones at the Lincoln Memorial, and she doesn't give a speech.
She sings: an old spiritual about being scorned and put down, slow and huge, and the crowd goes still.
A little later, Martin Luther King Jr. is speaking, and the story is told that she called out to him: tell them about the dream, Martin. However it happened, he moved away from his prepared text.

teach.b: Mahalia Jackson grew up in New Orleans and sang in church from childhood. She moved north to Chicago and kept singing, in storefront churches, at funerals, anywhere they'd have her.
Gospel music in that city was being shaped by people like Thomas A. Dorsey, a songwriter who had once played the blues.

teach.h: A SONG WRITTEN OUT OF GRIEF.
teach.b: Dorsey wrote the song behind today's carry: Precious Lord, Take My Hand. By his own account, he wrote it out of grief, after his wife and newborn child died.

It's a prayer from someone tired, barely standing, asking to be led home. She made it one of her signature songs. Offered good money to sing the blues, she turned it down; she would sing gospel and nothing else.
The song's plea is an old one in scripture.

teach.h: I WILL HOLD THY RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: In Isaiah, in the King James Bible, God says: "For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee."

And in Psalm seventy-three, someone who has nearly lost their footing says: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand." Hold my hand. A child says it crossing a street.

When Martin Luther King Jr. was killed, Mahalia Jackson sang Precious Lord at his funeral. The movement that had marched to her singing now grieved to it. Gospel, the way she sang it, was never only for Sunday.

teach.h: FROM THE MARCH TO THE FUNERAL.
teach.b: It walked into the march and into the funeral, and kept asking for a hand.

how: Gospel music is sung in Black churches across the United States and far beyond, by choirs and soloists in Sunday worship, at funerals and at community gatherings.

games.q: you're a gospel singer, and you're offered good money to sing the blues instead. what do you do?
o: take it: a singer has to eat.
sing both and see which sells.
turn it down and sing gospel only.
games.why: Mahalia Jackson turned it down. she would sing gospel and nothing else, and took it from the church into the street.

practice: Play Mahalia Jackson singing Precious Lord, Take My Hand, or any gospel recording you like, or read Isaiah's line slowly: I will hold thy right hand, fear not.

Rest one hand open on your knee, and notice where in your life you'd like a hand to hold. If you pray, let the song carry your own asking; if not, let a woman singing for tired people keep you company.

wordCard.voice: Mahalia Jackson. The queen of gospel, from New Orleans and Chicago, who sang at the Lincoln Memorial during the great march for jobs and freedom, and sang Precious Lord at King's funeral.

orig.note: Hebrew: the right hand — the hand God holds in Isaiah 41:13 and Psalm 73:23.

carryVoice: Your line: precious lord. A song for anyone too tired to stand. Day nine hundred ninety-three, done.
